client: I've been having a really hard time since my dad passed away about two months ago. I can't seem to focus at work at all — I'll sit down to do something simple and my mind just goes blank, or I get this wave of emotion that I can't push through. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because it feels like the kind of thing that just has to hurt until it doesn't anymore.
therapist: What you're carrying right now sounds truly heavy, and I want you to know that the difficulty concentrating, those waves of emotion at unexpected moments — those are very real and very normal responses to losing someone so important. You mentioned feeling like talking might not help, and I actually think that's worth gently exploring, because sometimes that thought itself — *"nothing can touch this pain"* — can quietly deepen the isolation around grief. What does it feel like for you when one of those waves hits at work — is there a particular thought or image that tends to come with it?

client: Sometimes it's triggered by something really small and stupid, like I'll see a notification on my phone and think "I should call Dad about this," and then it hits me all over again that I can't. It's like this split second where my brain forgets and then remembers, and that moment of forgetting almost makes it worse somehow. I end up just staring at my screen for a long time after that, feeling kind of hollow and useless.
therapist: That moment you're describing — the brief forgetting, and then the remembering — is one of the most quietly painful parts of grief, and there's nothing "small or stupid" about it at all; your brain is actually doing something very human in still reaching for him. I also want to gently notice the words you used about yourself afterward: "hollow and useless" — that's a pretty harsh way to describe someone who is simply in the middle of grieving. When that hollow feeling settles in after one of those moments, what kinds of thoughts do you tend to have about yourself?

client: Honestly, I think things like "you can't even hold it together for one workday" or "everyone else is managing their lives and you're falling apart over a phone notification." There's also this guilt underneath it, like I feel bad that I'm not being more productive, as if grieving is somehow a personal failing or a choice I'm making. I know that probably sounds irrational when I say it out loud, but in the moment it feels completely true.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you can already notice, even a little, that there's a gap between what that voice is telling you and what's actually true — that awareness is genuinely important. But I also hear that in the moment, the self-criticism feels completely convincing, and that guilt about grieving is sitting on top of an already painful loss, which is an exhausting weight to carry. I'm curious — if a close friend came to you and said they couldn't focus at work two months after losing their father, what would you actually think about them?

client: I'd think they were going through something really hard and that it made complete sense, I wouldn't judge them at all. But I know what you're getting at, and I want to be honest — when I try to turn that same thought toward myself, it just doesn't land the same way. It's like there's a rule that applies to everyone else but somehow doesn't apply to me, and I can see that's not logical, but I can't seem to close that gap just by pointing it out.
therapist: You're being so honest right now, and that actually matters a lot — because you're naming something really important: that *seeing* the double standard and *feeling* its unfairness are two very different things, and just pointing at the logic doesn't automatically heal the gap. That's not a failure of insight on your part; it's actually why grief and self-compassion are such slow, patient work rather than a puzzle to be solved in one moment. I'm wondering — where do you think that harsher rule about yourself comes from, the one that seems to exempt you from the same kindness you'd offer everyone else?

client: Honestly, I think part of it comes from my dad himself — he was someone who really valued pushing through, not complaining, getting things done no matter what. I grew up kind of absorbing that, and I think there's something really painful about the fact that the standard I'm failing to meet right now is basically his standard. It's like I'm disappointing him even in how I'm grieving him, which I realize sounds kind of twisted when I say it out loud.
therapist: What you just uncovered feels really significant — there's something deeply painful about carrying someone's values so close to your heart, and then feeling like you're falling short of them in the very moment you're mourning their loss. And I want to sit with that word you used, "disappointing him" — because the man whose standard you absorbed was also the father who, I imagine, loved you; and it's worth wondering whether he would truly look at his child grieving him and feel disappointment, or something else entirely. What do you think he would actually feel, if he could see you right now?

client: I think he'd probably feel sad, and maybe he'd want to tell me it's okay — but there's a part of me that can't fully believe that, because I never actually saw him give himself that kind of permission when he was struggling. It's hard to imagine him saying something he never really modeled, you know? And then I feel guilty for even analyzing him like this, like I'm criticizing him when he's not here to respond.
therapist: There's something really tender in what you just said — you're holding love and complexity about your dad at the same time, and that's not a betrayal of him, it's actually a very honest form of love. Noticing that he may not have had permission to be gentle with himself isn't a criticism; it might even be a kind of grief within the grief, mourning not just his absence but perhaps the softness that neither of you quite got to share. I'm wondering — is it possible that part of healing this might involve doing something he couldn't quite do for himself, and whether that could feel like honoring him rather than failing him?

client: That reframe is actually kind of stopping me in my tracks, because I hadn't thought about it that way at all. Like, maybe being gentler with myself isn't weakness or giving up on his values, but actually going further than he could go — there's something about that idea that feels both meaningful and really uncomfortable at the same time. I'm not sure I can just decide to believe it, though; it feels like the kind of thing that sounds right in this room but might fall apart the moment I'm back at my desk staring at that phone notification.
therapist: That tension you're feeling — where something resonates deeply but doesn't yet feel solid enough to hold onto in a hard moment — is actually a really honest and important place to be, and it means you're taking this seriously rather than just collecting a nice idea. You're right that insight often feels more fragile when we're back in the middle of real pain, which is why it helps to build small, concrete anchors rather than relying on the idea alone. I'm wondering — when that next notification moment comes and the hollow feeling hits, what might it look like to do something tiny, even just a few words, that treats yourself as someone going through something hard rather than someone failing?

client: I guess I could try saying something to myself in that moment, like "this is grief, not weakness" or something along those lines — but I'm already imagining doing it and feeling a little silly, like I'm just reciting a line that my brain won't actually buy into. I think my worry is that it becomes this mechanical thing I do that doesn't really touch the feeling, just kind of sits on top of it. Is there a way to make it feel less like a script and more like something real?
therapist: That concern is really worth taking seriously, because you're right that words can become hollow if they're just layered over a feeling rather than meeting it. One thing that sometimes makes the difference is pausing first to actually *acknowledge* the feeling before trying to reframe it — so instead of going straight to "this is grief, not weakness," it might start with something like "there it is again, that missing him" — just naming what's actually happening, which can make the next thought feel less like a script and more like a conversation with yourself. What do you think it would feel like to let the wave land for just a moment before responding to it, rather than trying to catch it on the way in?

client: Honestly, my instinct is to do the opposite of that — when the wave comes, I want to push through it as fast as possible so I can get back to functioning, because sitting at my desk at work and just letting myself feel it sounds kind of terrifying. I'm worried that if I actually let it land, I won't be able to pull myself back together, like opening a door I won't be able to close. I guess I don't fully trust that the wave has a natural end to it.
therapist: That fear makes complete sense — and it's actually one of the most common things that keeps grief feeling so overwhelming, because the very act of bracing against the wave can make it feel more endless and powerful than it might actually be. What you're describing, that worry about opening a door you can't close, is itself worth examining gently — because in my experience, and in what research on grief tends to show, waves do have a natural shape: they rise, peak, and fall, usually within minutes, even when it doesn't feel that way. I'm wondering if there's ever been a moment, even a small one, where you did let yourself feel something difficult and found that you did, eventually, come back to yourself?

client: Actually, yeah — the night after the funeral, I just completely broke down at home alone, and I remember thinking it was going to swallow me whole, but eventually I cried myself out and fell asleep and woke up the next morning still here. I hadn't really connected that to what you're describing until just now, but I guess that was the door opening and closing. It still feels different to think about doing that intentionally at work though, even in a small way — that felt like a private moment, and work feels like a place where I have to keep the door locked.
therapist: What you just remembered is really important — you lived through the door opening, and you came back, even on one of the hardest nights of your life, and some part of you knew that without quite having the words for it until now. And I hear you that work feels like a different world, one where vulnerability has to stay contained, and that's a real and legitimate boundary — nobody is asking you to grieve openly at your desk. I'm wondering if there might be a middle path, something very small and private, like stepping away for two minutes to a bathroom or a stairwell, where you could briefly let the wave land in a way that's still protected but doesn't require you to keep pushing it down all day?
